title: Penicillin and Alcohol: Can You Drink on Penicillin VK?
excerpt: Can you drink on penicillin? Why there's no dangerous reaction, whether alcohol makes it less effective, the Bicillin shot, allergy vs. alcohol flushing, and when to skip drinking entirely.
metaDescription: Can you drink on penicillin? Why there's no dangerous reaction, whether alcohol weakens it, the Bicillin shot, and when to skip alcohol completely.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** penicillin and alcohol do not have a dangerous chemical reaction. Unlike metronidazole, penicillin won't make you violently sick if you have a drink, and there is no good evidence that a moderate amount of alcohol stops penicillin from working. The common "never drink on antibiotics" rule is a blanket warning that fits some antibiotics far better than others, and penicillin is one of the gentler cases. That said, "not dangerous" is not the same as "a good idea." Alcohol can make penicillin's stomach side effects worse, disrupt the sleep your body needs to recover, and blur the line between a hangover and a drug reaction you should report.

**The quick rules:** If you feel unwell, skip the drink. If you feel mostly fine and want one or two drinks at a dinner, that is unlikely to cause harm for a healthy adult, but keep it light, eat first, drink water, and never skip or delay a dose. If you were given metronidazole or tinidazole along with penicillin, the rules change completely: no alcohol at all. And any new rash, swelling, or trouble breathing while on penicillin needs a doctor, whether or not you were drinking.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and prescribing guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and your prescription. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking if** you take other prescription medicines, have liver or kidney disease, are pregnant, have a history of seizures, or were prescribed more than one antibiotic. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** you develop swelling of the face, lips, or tongue, wheezing, trouble breathing, a widespread rash with blistering or peeling skin, or feel faint after a dose.

## Can You Drink Alcohol While Taking Penicillin?

For most healthy adults, a small amount of alcohol while taking penicillin is unlikely to cause a harmful interaction. That is the straightforward answer to the most searched question on this topic, and it's what most pharmacists will tell you if you ask directly.

Here's why. "Penicillin" usually means one of a few closely related drugs:

- **Penicillin VK (penicillin V potassium)**, the tablet or liquid most people get from a pharmacy. It's commonly prescribed for strep throat, some dental infections, and some skin infections, and it's usually taken two to four times a day for a set number of days (often 10 days for strep throat).
- **Benzathine penicillin G (sold as Bicillin L-A)**, a long-acting injection used for syphilis, some strep infections, and to prevent rheumatic fever from coming back.
- **Penicillin G given by IV**, which is used in hospitals for serious infections. If you're in hospital on IV antibiotics, you shouldn't be drinking anyway.

None of these are known to react with alcohol the way certain other antibiotics do. Alcohol is broken down in your liver mainly by enzymes called alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase. Penicillin is cleared mostly unchanged through your kidneys and doesn't block those liver enzymes. So the two mostly travel separate paths through your body, which is why there's no known "toxic" combination here.

### What "a small amount" means in practice

When pharmacists say an occasional drink is probably fine, they mean something like one standard drink, or two at most, with food, on a day you already feel better. A standard drink in the US is roughly a 12-ounce beer at 5% alcohol, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits. They do not mean a night out, a bottomless brunch, or drinking to the point of a hangover. Our guide to [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains how quickly your body clears each drink if you want to plan around your doses.

## Why Do Doctors Say "No Alcohol With Antibiotics" Then?

The blanket warning exists for a few good reasons, even though it isn't based on a specific penicillin-alcohol reaction.

**1. Some antibiotics really do react with alcohol.** Metronidazole (Flagyl) and tinidazole can cause what's called a disulfiram-like reaction: flushing, a pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, and a racing heart if you drink. A few less common antibiotics, such as certain cephalosporins given in hospital, can do something similar. Linezolid can interact with certain tap beers and red wines that contain a compound called tyramine. A simple "no alcohol with any antibiotic" rule is easier to remember than a list of exceptions, so many clinicians just say it across the board. Our overview of [antibiotics and alcohol](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) covers which ones matter most.

**2. You're sick.** You were given penicillin because you have an infection. Alcohol can interfere with sleep, dehydrate you, and, with heavy use, weaken parts of your immune response. None of that helps you get better faster. Our deep dive on [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) goes through the research.

**3. Drinking makes people forget doses.** Penicillin VK has a short half-life, which is why it's dosed several times a day. Missing doses, or taking them late after a night out, is a far more realistic way for alcohol to undermine your treatment than any chemical interaction.

**4. Old habits and lore.** There's a popular story that the rule dates back to World War II, when penicillin was so scarce that it was recovered from patients' urine, and beer drinking supposedly diluted it. Penicillin really was recycled this way in the early days, but the beer part is hard to verify and is best treated as folklore. Another commonly told story links the advice to sexual health clinics, which wanted patients treated for infections such as syphilis to avoid alcohol-fueled decisions during treatment. Either way, the advice has outlived the specific reasons behind it.

## Does Alcohol Make Penicillin Less Effective?

There is no good evidence that moderate drinking makes penicillin less effective. This is the second biggest question people ask, and it's worth a clear answer.

Penicillin works by damaging the cell walls of bacteria as they grow. Alcohol doesn't neutralize the drug, and in normal drinking amounts it doesn't meaningfully change how much of the drug gets into your blood or how long it stays there. We cover the broader question for all antibiotics in [does alcohol make antibiotics less effective?](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-make-antibiotics-less-effective)

Where alcohol can get in the way is indirect:

- **Missed or late doses.** Penicillin levels drop fairly quickly between doses, so timing matters more than it does for once-a-day antibiotics.
- **Vomiting.** If you throw up soon after a dose, you may not have absorbed it. Ask a pharmacist whether to repeat it rather than guessing.
- **Poor sleep and dehydration.** Both slow recovery and can make you feel like the antibiotic "isn't working" when the real issue is that your body is run down.
- **Heavy drinking.** Long-term heavy drinking is linked to higher rates of infections such as pneumonia and to slower recovery. That's a reason to cut back while you're sick, not a reason to panic about one glass of wine.

One more practical point: penicillin VK is absorbed best on an empty stomach, and many pharmacy labels say to take it an hour before or two hours after a meal. That can be awkward around a dinner with drinks. Follow the directions on your label, and if the timing clashes with your plans, ask your pharmacist how to space things rather than skipping a dose.

## Stomach Upset: The Side Effect Alcohol Makes Worse

The most common side effects of penicillin are digestive: nausea, an upset stomach, and loose stools or diarrhea. Antibiotics disturb the normal bacteria in your gut, and alcohol irritates the stomach lining and speeds things through your bowel. Put them together and a mild side effect can turn into a miserable day. If you're already dealing with this, our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains what's going on and how to recover.

Drink plenty of water, eat simple food, and hold off on alcohol until your stomach settles.

### When diarrhea needs a doctor

Most antibiotic-related diarrhea is mild and stops after the course ends. But antibiotics, including penicillins, can occasionally trigger an infection called *C. difficile*, which can be serious. **Call your doctor if you have** watery diarrhea several times a day for more than a day or two, diarrhea with blood or mucus, strong stomach cramps, or a fever. This can happen during treatment or even weeks after you finish. Don't take anti-diarrhea medicine for it without checking with a doctor first.

## Penicillin Allergy vs. an Alcohol Reaction: Don't Guess

This is the most important safety section on this page, and the one most articles skip.

Penicillin is one of the most common causes of drug allergy. Allergic reactions usually show up as hives, an itchy rash, or swelling, and in rare cases as anaphylaxis, a severe reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. Alcohol, meanwhile, can cause facial flushing, warmth, and in some people hives or a stuffy nose, especially in people with an [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) or a true [alcohol allergy](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy).

That overlap creates two risks:

1. **You blame the alcohol for a real penicillin allergy.** If you get hives after a drink and a dose, you might assume it's "just the wine" and keep taking the drug. Allergic reactions can get worse with repeated doses.
2. **You blame penicillin for an alcohol reaction.** If you flush after drinking and decide you're allergic to penicillin, you may carry a false allergy label for years. That matters because people with a penicillin allergy label are often given broader, less targeted antibiotics. The CDC notes that while about 10% of people in the US report a penicillin allergy, fewer than 1% of the population is truly allergic.

**What to do:** If you get any new rash or hives while taking penicillin, stop drinking and contact your doctor or pharmacist the same day, and don't take your next dose until you've spoken to someone. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room** if you have swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat, wheezing or trouble breathing, a hoarse voice, dizziness or fainting, or a rash that blisters or peels.

If you were once told you're allergic to penicillin but aren't sure why, ask your doctor about allergy testing. Many people turn out not to be allergic, especially if the reaction was years ago.

## The Penicillin Shot (Bicillin) and Alcohol

People who get a benzathine penicillin G injection, most often for syphilis, often ask whether they can drink afterward. There's no known chemical interaction between the injection and alcohol. Two things are still worth knowing.

**The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.** When syphilis is treated, some people develop a fever, chills, headache, and muscle aches within the first 24 hours. It happens as the bacteria die off and usually settles within a day. It's not an allergy, but it can feel a lot like a bad hangover or the flu. Drinking that night would make it harder to tell what's happening and harder to report it accurately. It's sensible to skip alcohol for at least the first day or two after the shot.

**Follow-up matters more than the drink.** Syphilis treatment usually comes with instructions about follow-up blood tests and avoiding sex until you and any partners are treated. Those instructions are what actually protect your health, so plan around them.

The injection is also painful for some people, and it's common to feel sore and tired afterward. Rest and water will do more for you than a drink.

## Penicillin VK for Strep Throat or a Dental Infection

These are two of the most common reasons people get penicillin VK, and both come with extra reasons to hold off on drinking.

**Strep throat.** A sore, swollen throat plus a fever is a recipe for dehydration. Alcohol stings inflamed tissue, dries out your mouth and throat, and adds to fluid loss. Strep throat usually improves within a day or two of starting antibiotics, but you need to finish the whole course (often 10 days) to clear the infection properly and lower the risk of complications. Don't stop early because you feel better and want to go out.

**Dental infections.** Dentists often prescribe penicillin VK for an infected tooth or after some procedures. Alcohol can irritate a healing socket or gum and may increase bleeding after an extraction. Some dental infections are treated with penicillin *plus* metronidazole, which is a combination where alcohol is genuinely off-limits (see the next section).

**Painkillers are the hidden issue.** Both conditions are commonly treated with over-the-counter pain relief alongside penicillin. Acetaminophen and alcohol together put extra strain on the liver, especially with repeated doses. Ibuprofen and alcohol together raise the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding. Read our guides to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) and [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) before combining them. The same goes for cold and cough products, many of which contain acetaminophen or sedating ingredients; our page on [cough medicine and alcohol](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol) covers what to watch for.

## When You Should Skip Alcohol Completely

The general "a drink is probably fine" answer doesn't apply in these situations.

### You were also prescribed metronidazole or tinidazole

This is the big one. Penicillin and metronidazole are sometimes prescribed together, for example for certain dental infections or abdominal infections. Metronidazole can cause a severe reaction with alcohol, and you need to avoid it during treatment and for at least 48 hours after your last dose (72 hours for tinidazole). Check every label in your bag. If you've already had a drink on metronidazole, read [what to do if you accidentally drank on metronidazole](/never-hungover/accidentally-drank-on-metronidazole), and see our full [metronidazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) guide.

### You feel properly unwell

Fever, chills, a pounding headache, or being wiped out by the infection all mean your body is busy. Alcohol will make you feel worse, may raise your heart rate, and will make it harder to notice if the infection is getting worse instead of better.

### You take other medicines that interact with alcohol

Sedatives, sleep aids, opioid painkillers, some antidepressants, seizure medicines, and blood thinners can all interact with alcohol in ways penicillin doesn't. The antibiotic isn't the issue in those cases; the rest of your medication list is. A pharmacist can check everything in a couple of minutes.

### You have liver or kidney disease, are pregnant, or have a seizure history

Penicillin is cleared by the kidneys, so people with reduced kidney function may need dose adjustments. Alcohol adds load to the liver. Pregnancy changes the advice on alcohol entirely. Very high doses of penicillin, usually only in hospital settings and in people with kidney problems, have been linked to seizures, and alcohol can lower the seizure threshold too. In any of these situations, ask your doctor directly.

## How Long After Penicillin Can I Drink?

For penicillin on its own, there's no official waiting period, because there's no reaction that requires one. In practice, most people do best by waiting until:

1. **You've finished the full course.** This removes any risk of missed or delayed doses.
2. **You feel back to normal.** No fever, no stomach upset, eating and sleeping normally.
3. **You've checked your other prescriptions.** If anything else you were given has its own alcohol rule (metronidazole being the main one), follow the stricter rule.

If you have an event during your course and you feel fine, a single drink with food is unlikely to hurt. Just keep your dosing schedule intact. Set a phone alarm if you need to.

## Penicillin Side Effects That Can Look Like a Hangover

It's easy to confuse the two, so here's how they line up.

| Symptom | Could be a hangover | Could be penicillin | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nausea or upset stomach | Yes | Yes, common | Eat bland food, sip water, skip alcohol |
| Loose stools | Yes | Yes, common | Call a doctor if watery and frequent, bloody, or with fever |
| Headache | Yes | Sometimes | Hydrate; check painkiller labels before taking one |
| Flushing or warm face | Yes | Less common | Watch for hives or swelling, which point to allergy |
| Hives, itchy rash | Sometimes | Yes, a sign of allergy | Stop and call your doctor; 911 if breathing or swelling issues |
| Fever and chills | Rarely | Can be Jarisch-Herxheimer after a syphilis shot, or the infection itself | Contact your clinic, especially if it lasts beyond a day |
| Black or "furry" tongue, mouth thrush | No | Occasional | Mention it to your doctor or pharmacist |

When in doubt, assume it's worth a call. Pharmacists answer these questions all day and won't think you're overreacting.

## A Sensible Plan If You Have an Event Mid-Course

If a wedding, birthday, or work dinner falls in the middle of your prescription, here's a practical approach:

- **Ask yourself honestly how you feel.** If you're still feverish or run down, sit this one out or stick to non-alcoholic drinks.
- **Plan your doses first.** Work out when your doses fall that day and night, and set reminders. Don't let a late night push a dose to the next morning.
- **Eat a proper meal** and alternate every drink with a glass of water.
- **Cap it at one or two drinks.** This isn't the night for shots or a long session.
- **Check your other meds.** Skip any acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or sleep aids until the alcohol has cleared, and read labels on anything you take for a sore throat or cold.
- **Get to bed at a reasonable time.** Sleep is part of the treatment.

Our general guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) has more habits with good evidence behind them.

## Where Supplements Fit (and Where They Don't)

People who search for penicillin and alcohol sometimes ask whether a hangover supplement makes drinking during treatment "safer." It doesn't. No supplement changes how penicillin works, cancels out the effect alcohol has on recovery, or protects you from an allergic reaction.

For the times when you're healthy and not on antibiotics, some people use DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited data in people, so think of it as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers outright, and it is not a reason to drink more. If you want to try it after you've recovered, a popular option is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical doses and timing. If you take prescription medicines regularly, our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known, and the honest summary is that supplement interactions are poorly studied, so tell your pharmacist what you take.

## Related Antibiotic Guides

If you've been given a different antibiotic, the answer may be different. Amoxicillin is a close relative of penicillin and behaves much the same way with alcohol; see [amoxicillin and alcohol](/never-hungover/amoxicillin-and-alcohol). For other common prescriptions, see our guides to [cephalexin and alcohol](/never-hungover/cephalexin-and-alcohol), [azithromycin and alcohol](/never-hungover/azithromycin-and-alcohol), and [doxycycline and alcohol](/never-hungover/doxycycline-and-alcohol).

## The Bottom Line

Penicillin and alcohol don't have a dangerous chemical interaction, and a drink or two is unlikely to stop the antibiotic from working. The real risks are indirect: worse stomach side effects, poorer sleep, missed doses, confusion between a hangover and an allergic reaction, and painkillers or other medicines that do clash with alcohol. The simplest plan is to wait until you've finished the course and feel well. If you do drink mid-course, keep it light, eat first, keep every dose on time, and never drink if metronidazole or tinidazole is part of your treatment. Any new rash, swelling, or trouble breathing needs medical attention right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking penicillin?**

For most healthy adults, a drink or two while taking penicillin is unlikely to cause a dangerous reaction. Penicillin does not have the severe alcohol reaction that metronidazole and tinidazole do, and moderate drinking is not known to stop it working. The better advice is still to skip alcohol, or keep it light, until you feel well, because alcohol can worsen stomach side effects, disrupt sleep, and slow your recovery. Check with your doctor or pharmacist if you take other medicines or have liver disease.

**Does alcohol make penicillin less effective?**

There is no good evidence that moderate drinking makes penicillin stop working. Alcohol does not break down the drug or block it from reaching the infection in any meaningful way. The real risks are indirect: heavy drinking can make you forget or vomit up doses, worsen sleep, and strain your immune system, all of which can slow recovery. Taking every dose on schedule matters far more than one drink.

**How long after taking penicillin can I drink alcohol?**

There is no official waiting period for penicillin alone, because it does not cause the reaction that requires a gap with metronidazole. Many people choose to wait until they have finished the full course and feel back to normal. If you were also given metronidazole or tinidazole, follow that drug's rule instead: no alcohol during treatment and for at least 48 hours after the last metronidazole dose (72 hours for tinidazole).

**Can I drink after a penicillin shot (Bicillin)?**

A long-acting penicillin injection such as benzathine penicillin G (Bicillin L-A) is not known to react with alcohol. It is often used for syphilis, and some people get a fever, chills, headache, and muscle aches within a day of treatment (the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction). Alcohol would make that day harder and could hide symptoms you should report, so it is sensible to avoid drinking for at least the first day or two and follow your clinic's instructions.

**Is it safe to drink on penicillin VK for strep throat or a dental infection?**

Penicillin VK has no direct dangerous interaction with alcohol, but drinking is rarely a good idea with a sore throat or a dental infection. Alcohol can sting inflamed tissue, worsen dehydration if you have a fever, and interfere with sleep. Many dental and throat infections are also treated with painkillers, and acetaminophen or ibuprofen each carry their own alcohol warnings. Finish the full course and wait until you feel well before drinking.

**Is a rash after drinking on penicillin an allergic reaction?**

It could be either, and you should not guess. Alcohol can cause flushing and, in some people, hives, while penicillin is a common cause of drug allergy rashes. Stop drinking and contact your doctor or pharmacist about any new rash while on penicillin. Call 911 or go to an emergency room right away if you have swelling of the face, lips, or tongue, trouble breathing, wheezing, or feel faint.

**Does DHM interact with penicillin?**

There are no known reports of DHM interacting with penicillin, but supplement interactions are poorly studied, so tell your pharmacist about anything you take. DHM does not make it safer to drink while you are fighting an infection, and there is no good evidence that it affects how penicillin works. If you are sick enough to need antibiotics, rest and fluids matter more than any supplement.
